input:
## Current use

This assessment takes a detailed and comprehensive look at how energy is used at the dairy plant, with a view to understanding the current position and identifying where worthwhile savings could potentially be made. The plant currently uses 3857 MWh of electricity per year, which is a very considerable amount of energy indeed. Within that overall total, refrigeration emerges as the load taking the largest share of electricity, which is perhaps not surprising for a dairy, where milk has to be cooled promptly after it arrives and finished products have to be kept cold in store. Steam is the other major energy stream on the site, and it is used for duties such as pasteurisation and for producing the hot water that cleaning regimes depend upon. Both streams are considered in this assessment, and an opportunity around heat recovery features prominently as the analysis develops. Energy is woven into every stage of the dairy's work, from the intake of raw milk through processing and packaging to the cold storage of the finished product, so a careful look at where it goes is a worthwhile exercise in its own right.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest single consumer of electricity at the plant, and it is a load that the dairy simply cannot do without. Raw milk must be cooled soon after collection and held cold, and the cold stores for finished product run continuously as well, so the refrigeration plant works hard each and every day of the year. The compressors remove heat from the cold rooms and the milk cooling duty, and that heat is then rejected at the condensers, where under present arrangements it is simply thrown away. It is worth pausing on this point, because it means the plant is simultaneously spending a great deal of electricity in order to dispose of heat, even while it buys in energy elsewhere on the site to produce heat for other purposes. The load is also a steady one across the year, since milk arrives and is processed in every season, and this steadiness makes the rejected heat a dependable stream to work with when heat recovery is being considered, rather than an intermittent one that appears and disappears with the weather.

## Steam

Steam serves a range of essential heating duties at the dairy, most notably the pasteurisation of milk and the production of hot water for the cleaning of vessels, pipework and plant, cleaning being a duty that a food site can never treat lightly. It is important to note, however, that the steam figures available for this assessment come from one winter month only, which places an important limitation on how far they can be generalised. Winter is the season in which incoming water is coldest and heating requirements are generally at their highest, so a single winter month is likely to give an inflated impression of the steam demand that prevails over the course of a full year. This seasonal caveat is flagged here and is taken into account again when the recommendation is reached, since a decision of this size deserves foundations that are as solid as they can reasonably be made.

## Recommendation

Pulling the threads together, this assessment has considered a heat-recovery retrofit in which the heat rejected by the refrigeration plant would be captured and reused elsewhere on the site, for example to preheat water that would otherwise be heated directly. The retrofit is projected to save 11% of the plant's electricity use of 3857 MWh per year, amounting to a saving of 424 MWh per year. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, that saving is worth $50912 per year. Against this, the capital cost of the retrofit is $762k, which gives a simple payback period of 15 years, a lengthy period by any standard. On top of that, the steam side of the analysis rests on one winter month of figures, with all of the seasonal uncertainty that involves. All things considered, the sensible course would seem to be to put the capital commitment on hold for the time being, while steam and refrigeration loads are monitored over a complete year so that the appraisal can be revisited on the basis of much firmer evidence. The opportunity itself remains a genuine one, and a fresh look at the numbers once a full year of data is in hand may yet paint a different picture.

## Current use

The plant uses 3857 MWh of electricity per year, and refrigeration takes the largest share of that use. A heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration plant is the measure under assessment: it is projected to cut electricity use, but the capital cost is repaid only over a long period, and the steam figures behind the assessment rest on one winter month. The sections below give the use position, the refrigeration position, and the limit on the steam data; the recommendation closes the assessment.

Electricity is metered for the whole site and the annual total is firm. The split between loads is not separately metered; the refrigeration share is the largest by the plant's running records, and no figure in this assessment turns on the exact split. Electricity use follows the milk intake: cooling, processing, and cold storage all run when milk is being handled, and milk arrives in every month. Steam is the second stream, serving pasteurisation and the hot water that cleaning depends on, and steam use has no annual metered total.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration runs in every month of the year. Raw milk is cooled on arrival and held cold, finished product is held in cold store, and both duties follow the milk intake, which does not stop with the seasons. The plant removes heat at its evaporators and rejects the heat at its condensers, where it is currently discharged and lost. A refrigeration plant is a heat source as well as a cooling source, and here the rejected heat is steady because the load behind it is steady. The cold chain also cannot be traded against the recovery scheme: the cooling temperatures are set by the product, and any arrangement that recovered heat at the cost of cooling performance would fail on the dairy's first duty. The retrofit is assessed on heat that is rejected after the cooling has been done, and on no other basis.

The retrofit recovers heat at the condensers and delivers it to duties otherwise heated directly, the preheating of cleaning water being the first such duty on this site. A dairy heats water in quantity and on a daily rhythm set by its cleaning cycles, so the demand for heat and the production of rejected heat are at least driven by the same working day. Recovery does not change the cooling provided; it changes the destination of heat the plant already moves. Its limit sits on the demand side: recovered heat has value only where a heated duty can take it when it is produced, and that match has not been established hour by hour. The projected saving is therefore built on annual totals, not on a metered match.

## Steam

Steam figures for the plant come from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal. The month carries the year's coldest incoming water and its highest heating demand on top of the process load of pasteurisation and cleaning, so read as a typical month it overstates steam use across the year. No annual steam figure is stated, because none has been measured. The process part of the steam load, the heating of milk and of cleaning water, follows production and is steadier than the total suggests; the seasonal part rides on top of it in the water temperature and the building load, and one month's figure mixes the two inseparably.

The limit bears on the retrofit in one direction: recovered heat displaces direct heating, and its value depends on how much direct heating the site does over a full year. A winter-only record inflates that value. The electricity saving stands on metered data; the steam picture behind it does not, and the recommendation keeps the two apart.

## Recommendation

The retrofit is projected to save 11% of electricity use, a saving of 424 MWh per year on the metered base of 3857 MWh per year. At $0.12 per kWh the saving is $50912 per year, against a capital cost of $762k: a simple payback of 15 years. Site management should not commit the capital on these figures. The payback outruns the period over which the tariff and the load can be forecast, and part of the case rests on steam data that one winter month cannot support.

The appraisal is a simple-payback appraisal. It charges the capital in the year it is spent and credits the saving at today's tariff in every later year, with no allowance for the cost of the money or for maintaining the new plant. That roughness does not drive the result: a case that fails on simple payback at this length is not restored by refinements that mostly charge it more, and the metering recommendation stands independently of the appraisal method.

The next step belongs to the plant's engineering manager: meter the steam system and the refrigeration load through a full year, and re-run the appraisal on that record. The metering should be specified to answer the open question as well, whether the rejected heat and the site's demand for heat coincide closely enough through the working day for the projected saving to be collected. The candidate measure is unchanged, and the refrigeration load that makes it attractive is not in question. The missing piece is annual evidence, and the decision should wait for it.
